newsitem.title: KENYA: Burundi mission cancelled by African ministers.
newsitem.headline: Burundi mission cancelled by African ministers.

text.p: African ministers cancelled on Wednesday a peace mission to Burundi because Burundi military strongman Pierre Buyoya has refused to negotiate with Hutu rebels fighting his army junta, a Kenyan minister said.

The cancellation announced by Kenyan Foreign Minister Kalonzo Musyoka marks an escalation in a standoff between Buyoya's isolated government and regional heads of state determined he restores constitutional legality to the country where ethnic war has killed 150,000 in three years.

"We have called off the mission following consultations. It is not opportune for us to go ahead with the mission. In the meantime the sanctions will continue," Musyoka said by telephone from the Tanzanian capital Dar es Salaam.

Musyoka told Reuters Burundi's declaration on Monday that it would defy regional leaders who are demanding that the army junta talks to Hutu rebels had jeopardised the mission and the region would now continue with crippling sanctions on Burundi.

The ministerial group appointed at last Saturday's heads of state summit in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha comprised of foreign ministers from Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Rwanda, Cameroon, Zaire and Zambia. It was to assess the junta's commitment to dialogue to end ethnic war.
"If Buyoya had the slightest respect for international opinion and the regional heads of state, then his government would not have issued the statement rejecting talks," Musyoka added.
"The ball is now really in his (Buyoya's) court. His approach is not helpful. We urge him to reconsider his position," said Musyoka.
The cancellation on Wednesday also followed security concerns for the group raised by Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa on Tuesday.

The ministers had met behind closed doors in Dar es Salaam on Tuesday to plot the next move against Burundi but Musyoka was non-committal on what they decided apart from saying the embargo would continue.
African leaders told Buyoya on Saturday to open unconditional talks with Hutu rebels within a month or face further sanctions.

Defying a U.S. suggestion to ease the embargo, now more than two months old, regional leaders decided to send a ministerial committee to Burundi to check on Buyoya's commitment to unconditional negotiations stated in a letter from him to the Arusha summit meeting.

At their latest summit in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha on Saturday, the regional leaders gave Burundi one month to enter negotiations with Leonard Nyangoma's Forces for the Defence of Democracy (FDD) and smaller Hutu armed factions.

The leaders from Cameroun, Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda, Tanzania, Zambia, Zaire and the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) warned of penalties against any group in Burundi which refuses to negotiate within a month.
The leaders also refused to ease economic and transport sanctions against Burundi until Buyoya began talks with rebels fighting his Tutsi military junta.

But the leader of Burundi's main Tutsi opposition party on Tuesday hailed Buyoya's move to reject talks with the rebels and attacked Tanzania and Kenya -- main actors in Saturday's move to maintain sanctions -- as countries bent on hitting Burundi.
The embargo was imposed on landlocked Burundi on July 31 as punishment for the military coup six days earlier which ousted Hutu president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya and installed Buyoya.
